To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the increased expression of MCH-I and B- 7 molecules on the cell membrane of glioma cells transfected with antisense IGF -I cDNA, is a possible mechanism of immune recognition of gliomas by the host immune system.
the expression of MHC- I and B-7 by transfected glioma cells could contribute to the immune recognition and rejection of the tumor.

(1) glioma cells, when transfected with IGF-I antisense mRNA, express MHC-I molecules and B-7 co-signaling molecules, (2) this expression is associated with an increased immune recognition, (3) this recognition is mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic lymphocytes, and (4) this immune recognition is tumor specific.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a new approach for the treatment of brain tumors.
the identification of new strategies for the treatment of brain tumors, which are characterized by a high degree of immunogenicity.
the development of a gene therapy approach to gliomas based on the expression of an antisense mRNA for IGF-I.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the increased expression of MCH-I and B-77 molecules is the final result of the IGF-I downregulation in the transfected cells.

the expression of IGF-I antisense mRNA in rat C-6, human primary gliomas and mouse teratoma cells is able to induce the expression of MHC I and B-7 co-signaling molecules, thus contributing to the immune recognition of gliomas and to the development of a tumor-specific immune response.
the IGF-I antisense vector is able to induce the expression of MHC I and of co-signalling B7 molecules in the transfected glioma cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IGF-I is a tumor antigen and its expression is a critical factor for the immune recognition of gliomas.
IGF-I is a major factor for the growth of malignant tumors, including gliomas, but also a key factor for tumor immunogenicity and immune escape.
IGF-I is a major factor involved in the immune escape of glioma, and that IGF-I down-regulation may be useful for glioma immunotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of antisense IGF-1 cDNA in tumor cells induces an increase of MHC-I molecules and co-signaling B7 molecules.
IGF-I antisense RNA expression in glioma cells may induce the expression of MHC I and of co-signalling B-7 molecules and that these cells may be recognized by CD8+ lymphocyte mediated cytotoxicity.
the IGF-I antisense vector is a useful tool to generate tumor specific immunogenic cells.
